author.name: Sophocles
author.biography: Sophocles combined a long theatrical career with public responsibilities in Athens. His plays place people inside duties that can conflict without becoming trivial. Knowing what one ought to do does not guarantee knowing what that action will mean to everyone else. Sophocles wrote for a city that asked citizens to judge arguments in public. Antigone brings the competing claims of family, religion and civic authority into a dispute no institution can make painless.

hook.text: When would you break the law because obeying it would be wrong?

paragraphs: Creon has forbidden the burial of a man he considers an enemy of the city. Antigone regards the dead man as her brother, and burial as a duty no ruler can cancel.

Both understand their position as an obligation. Creon wants public authority to survive civil conflict. Antigone refuses to let political classification decide what she owes the dead. Their confrontation becomes dangerous partly because each believes that yielding would betray something larger than personal preference.

Sophocles gives courage an uncomfortable companion: the inability to hear a warning. Who gets to interpret divine duty? When does defending order become defending one's own authority? What happens to everyone nearby when two people make compromise a form of disgrace?

Read for the quieter voices trying to open a space between surrender and collision. We admire people who stand by their principles. How do we recognise when that admiration has stopped us asking what those principles require us to see?

orientation.text: The play follows a civil conflict in Thebes. Creon is the new ruler; Antigone and Ismene are sisters, and Haemon is Creon's son.
